# Why this warmup?

We almost never observe a complete surface.

We work with partial observations:

```text
points
pixels
samples
segments
training areas
time steps
```

Still, we make spatial statements about continuous areas.

## Core problem

A map is rarely a direct measurement.

It is usually a controlled translation from discrete observations into a spatial claim.

```text
discrete observations -> model assumption -> spatial output
```

Microclimate is used here as an example.

The workflow logic is more general.

# Course connection

This warmup connects several parts of the course.

```text
Sampling           Which observations do we have?
Drone / LiDAR      Which spatial structure can we observe?
Segmentation       Which spatial units do we create?
Regression         Which patterns can we transfer?
Classification     Which type occurs where?
Interpolation      What can we claim between observations?
Validation         How reliable is the spatial claim?
```

The focus is not interpolation as a tool.

The focus is spatial modelling under incomplete observation.

# Live goal

A short R script is read and executed during the session.

The workflow makes one step visible:

```text
point measurements -> spatial result raster
```

The display is not the main point.

The modelling assumption behind the display is the main point.

# Why scripts?

Scripts make spatial analyses reproducible.

They document:

```text
data
parameters
interpretation domain
model assumption
result
```

This matters for large data sets, repeated runs and later corrections.

# Starting point

Measurement stations provide point values.

The research question refers to space.

Between both stands a space-filling operation:

```text
What is assumed between the measurement points?
```

## Example context

Microclimate varies over short distances.

Possible controls include:

```text
elevation
terrain form
vegetation
shade
surface cover
cold-air drainage
```

This exercise deliberately reduces the case to temperature and elevation.

# Required data

The project contains:

```text
data/climdata.rds
data/DEM1.tif
```

`climdata.rds` contains stations and temperature columns.

`DEM1.tif` contains elevation as a raster.

## Code: load data

```r
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(gstat)
library(randomForest)

m   <- readRDS("data/climdata.rds")
dem <- rast("data/DEM1.tif")
names(dem) <- "altitude"
```

# One time step

The warmup uses one measurement time step:

```text
A20230830
```

All result rasters therefore refer to the same measurement situation.

## Code: set target variable

```r
m$temp <- m[["A20230830"]]
```

# Spatial reference

Points and raster must use the same CRS.

Otherwise elevation, distance and overlay cannot be interpreted consistently.

## Code: CRS and station elevation

```r
m <- st_transform(m, crs(dem))
m$altitude <- terra::extract(dem, terra::vect(m))$altitude

pts <- m[!is.na(m$temp) & !is.na(m$altitude),
         c("temp", "altitude")]
```

# Interpretation domain

The results are not produced for the whole DEM.

The valid domain is:

```text
convex hull of the stations + 20 m buffer
```

This limits interpretation to the sampled area.

## Code: interpretation domain

```r
area <- st_sf(
  geometry = st_buffer(
    st_convex_hull(st_union(st_geometry(pts))),
    20
  )
)

dem <- crop(dem, vect(area))
dem <- mask(dem, vect(area))
names(dem) <- "altitude"
```

# Prediction grid

The models predict for raster cells.

The DEM is converted into a table:

```text
cell
x
y
altitude
```

## Code: raster cells as target locations

```r
grid <- as.data.frame(dem, xy = TRUE, cells = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE)
names(grid)[4] <- "altitude"
grid <- grid[!is.na(grid$altitude), ]

grid_sf <- st_as_sf(
  grid,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs = st_crs(pts),
  remove = FALSE
)
```

# Four model ideas

The same measurements lead to four spatial result rasters.

```text
Voronoi      nearest station
IDW          local distance
LM altitude  elevation relation
RF warning   data-driven spatial/elevation partition
```

# Voronoi

Voronoi means:

```text
nearest station wins
```

Each raster cell receives the value of its nearest station.

This is transparent, but coarse.

## Code: Voronoi / nearest station

```r
vor_df <- gstat::idw(
  temp ~ 1,
  locations = pts,
  newdata = grid_sf,
  nmax = 1
)

map_vor <- make_map(vor_df$var1.pred, "Voronoi")
```

# IDW

IDW uses spatial proximity.

```text
near stations count more than distant stations
```

With `nmax = 4`, the estimate remains local.

## Code: IDW

```r
idw_df <- gstat::idw(
  temp ~ 1,
  locations = pts,
  newdata = grid_sf,
  nmax = 4
)

map_idw <- make_map(idw_df$var1.pred, "IDW")
```

# LM altitude

LM altitude uses elevation as predictor.

```text
temperature is transferred to raster cells through elevation
```

This is not a neighbourhood model.

## Code: LM altitude

```r
fit_lm <- lm(temp ~ altitude, data = st_drop_geometry(pts))

map_lm <- predict(dem, fit_lm)
names(map_lm) <- "LM_altitude"
```

# RF warning

RF also predicts temperature.

Input variables are:

```text
x
y
altitude
```

The model can flexibly partition location and elevation.

## Code: RF warning

```r
xy <- st_coordinates(pts)
pts$x <- xy[, 1]
pts$y <- xy[, 2]

fit_rf <- randomForest(
  temp ~ x + y + altitude,
  data = st_drop_geometry(pts),
  ntree = 200
)

rf_pred <- predict(fit_rf, newdata = grid)
map_rf <- make_map(rf_pred, "RF_warning")
```

# Why RF warning?

RF can produce a low error with very few stations.

This does not automatically mean:

```text
robust microclimatic explanation
```

It may simply mean:

```text
good adaptation to this specific point configuration
```

# Validation

Leave-one-out cross-validation:

```text
remove one station
fit the model with the remaining stations
predict the omitted station
store the error
```

## RMSE

$$
RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2}
$$

RMSE measures prediction error at station locations.

RMSE does not prove the process validity of the whole result raster.

# Validate LM and RF

LM and RF are checked with a visible loop.

This is intentionally simple to read.

## Code: LOOCV for LM and RF

```r
rmse_fun <- function(e) sqrt(mean(e * e, na.rm = TRUE))

lm_cv <- rep(NA, nrow(pts))
rf_cv <- rep(NA, nrow(pts))

for (i in 1:nrow(pts)) {
  train <- pts[-i, ]
  test  <- pts[i, ]

  fit_lm_i <- lm(temp ~ altitude, data = st_drop_geometry(train))
  lm_cv[i] <- predict(fit_lm_i, newdata = st_drop_geometry(test))

  fit_rf_i <- randomForest(
    temp ~ x + y + altitude,
    data = st_drop_geometry(train),
    ntree = 200
  )
  rf_cv[i] <- predict(fit_rf_i, newdata = st_drop_geometry(test))
}
```

# Validate Voronoi and IDW

For the `gstat` models, `gstat.cv()` performs LOOCV.

Important:

```text
validation and result generation use the same neighbourhood assumption
```

## Code: gstat.cv

```r
vor_model <- gstat(
  temp ~ 1,
  locations = pts,
  nmax = 1,
  set = list(idp = 2)
)

idw_model <- gstat(
  temp ~ 1,
  locations = pts,
  nmax = 4,
  set = list(idp = 2)
)

vor_cv <- gstat.cv(vor_model, nfold = nrow(pts))
idw_cv <- gstat.cv(idw_model, nfold = nrow(pts))
```

# RMSE table

The table is not an automatic method ranking.

It is a starting point for model criticism.

## Code: compute RMSE

```r
rmse <- data.frame(
  model = c("LM altitude", "Voronoi", "IDW", "RF warning"),
  RMSE = c(
    rmse_fun(pts$temp - lm_cv),
    rmse_fun(vor_cv$residual),
    rmse_fun(idw_cv$residual),
    rmse_fun(pts$temp - rf_cv)
  )
)

print(rmse)
```

# Result display

All result rasters are displayed with the same colour scale.

The measurement points are overlaid.

This shows both the spatial pattern and its measurement support.

## Code: display

```r
maps <- c(map_vor, map_idw, map_lm, map_rf)
z <- range(c(pts$temp - 1, pts$temp + 1), na.rm = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (i in 1:nlyr(maps)) {
  plot(maps[[i]], range = z, main = names(maps)[i])
  points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.8)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

# Result logic

```text
Voronoi      hard station territories
IDW          local neighbourhood
LM altitude  elevation relation
RF warning   data-driven partition
```

The display is only the surface.

The spatial claim lies in the model assumption.

# Discussion

Guiding questions:

```text
Which result shows hard station territories?
Which result shows local distance?
Which result mainly follows elevation?
Which result looks good, but remains risky?
Why is RMSE alone not enough?
```

# Conclusion

A spatial result does not emerge neutrally from point measurements.

Between observation and claim stand:

```text
interpretation domain
model assumption
predictors
validation
process plausibility
```

The script makes this chain visible in minimal form.
